Orthopedics · published research

Patellofemoral pain syndrome

One PBM trial found reduced pain during jump landing but no broad questionnaire or physical-test benefit; a separate HILT trial and pooled reviews do not establish a PBM-specific effect.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One PBM trial found reduced pain during jump landing but no broad questionnaire or physical-test benefit; a separate HILT trial and pooled reviews do not establish a PBM-specific effect.

Summary of the Evidence

A narrow mapping across the patellofemoral-pain subcategory and directly relevant knee-pain records identifies four titles: two randomized clinical trials and two meta-analyses. One clinical trial tests PBM and the other uses high-intensity laser therapy. The pooled reviews synthesize overlapping studies, so they do not represent additional participant cohorts.

Human and clinical evidence

In a 30-person randomized trial among young women with patellofemoral pain, PBM reduced pain during jump landing, but the study did not find a broad advantage on functional questionnaires or physical tests (Pocai et al. 2021). A separate randomized trial found better pain, knee flexion, and function with high-intensity laser plus exercise than with ultrasound-based comparators, but this tests a different modality and is not PBM evidence (Ozlu and Atilgan 2024). One 2025 meta-analysis of eight trials estimated pain and function gains but rated evidence very low; a 2026 analysis of four trials found a nonsignificant pain trend with substantial heterogeneity (Alayat et al. 2025 Chen et al. 2026).

Animal evidence

No relevant animal study was identified in the narrow patellofemoral-pain mapping.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone cell, tissue, or ex-vivo study was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The PBM trial used 590-nm visible yellow and 830-nm near-infrared light in young women. The HILT trial used a high-intensity protocol with different treatment characteristics. Diagnosis, age, activity, comparators, and outcome measures differ, so results should not be pooled as though they test one light intervention.

Interpretation

The direct PBM result is specific to pain during one task and does not show general improvement in function. Reviews and the HILT trial add context but do not establish a PBM effect across patellofemoral pain.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for task-specific pain reduction with PBM in patellofemoral pain Very low for broad function or durable benefit
Publications and records4 unique titles in a narrow patellofemoral-specific mapping

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The narrow mapping includes one PBM randomized trial, one high-intensity laser trial, and two pooled reviews that combine overlapping studies. The PBM trial found an effect on pain during one task but not across broader questionnaires or physical tests. A larger sham-controlled PBM trial with common functional outcomes would improve confidence.
